subject: physics
question_text: Define coefficient of viscosity. State Stokes' law. Explain the terminal velocity attained by a freely falling body (raindrop) in a viscous medium using a graph.

mark_split.label: Weight and upthrust in terms of r
Terminal velocity and its r² law

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Long Answer Question 3 (printed p.111). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The eight 1-mark step split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: η = F/(A·dv/dx) with SI unit N s m⁻² and dimensional formula [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]; Stokes' law F = 6πηrv for a small sphere in streamline flow; the raindrop's weight (4/3)πr³ρg and upthrust (4/3)πr³σg from the same volume; the balance 6πηrv_t = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g solves to v_t = (2/9)r²g(ρ − σ)/η, proportional to r², all matching the standard NCERT Class-11 Mechanical Properties of Fluids treatment.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The viscous force between layers
lines: Consider a fluid flowing in layers,
one layer sliding over the next.
Each layer exerts a tangential
force on the layer next to it,
opposing the relative motion
between them.
This viscous force is proportional
to the area of contact A and to
the velocity gradient dv/dx
between the layers:
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that the force is tangential, opposes relative motion, and depends on the area and the velocity gradient.
steps.why: This force law is the physical fact the coefficient of viscosity is defined from — without it, η has no formula to come from.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the velocity gradient dv/dx and stating the force depends only on the area.
Describing the force as acting between the fluid and a solid wall rather than between two layers of the fluid itself.

recall.must_convey: That the viscous force between two fluid layers is tangential, opposes their relative motion, and is proportional to the area of contact and the velocity gradient: F = ηA(dv/dx).
accept: viscous force is tangential and opposes relative motion
force depends on area and velocity gradient
F equals eta A dv by dx
layers exert a tangential force on each other
reject: F equals six pi eta r v
heard_as: F equals eta A dv dx

steps.memory_tip: Layers dragging on layers: the force needs both an area and a velocity gradient.

steps.label: Defining the coefficient of viscosity
lines: Rearranging the force law defines
the coefficient of viscosity:
η is the tangential force per unit
area per unit velocity gradient.
SI unit: N s m⁻², the pascal
second. CGS unit: the poise.
Dimensional formula: [ML⁻¹T⁻¹].
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Give the formula for η in words, then its SI unit, CGS unit and dimensional formula.
steps.why: A defined quantity is only complete once its unit and dimensions are stated alongside its formula.
common_mistakes: Stating only the SI unit and leaving out the dimensional formula [ML⁻¹T⁻¹].
Writing the formula as η = FA/(dv/dx) instead of η = F/(A·dv/dx) — the area divides, it does not multiply.

recall.must_convey: That the coefficient of viscosity η is the tangential force per unit area per unit velocity gradient, η = F/(A·dv/dx), with SI unit N s per metre squared, CGS unit the poise, and dimensional formula M L inverse T inverse.
accept: eta equals F over A dv dx
force per unit area per unit velocity gradient
SI unit is newton second per metre squared
dimensional formula M L inverse T inverse
reject: F equals six pi eta r v

steps.memory_tip: η is force per area per velocity gradient — divide by both.

steps.label: Stokes' law — the conditions
lines: Stokes' law gives the viscous drag
on a small sphere moving through a
fluid.
It holds when the sphere is small
and moves slowly, so that the flow
of fluid around it stays
streamline.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. State both conditions: a small sphere, moving slowly, so the flow around it stays streamline.
steps.why: Stokes' law is not universal — it is derived for streamline flow around the sphere, so the conditions have to be stated before the formula is used.
common_mistakes: Giving the formula without stating the streamline-flow condition it depends on.
Saying Stokes' law holds for any sphere at any speed.

recall.must_convey: That Stokes' law holds for a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid, so that the flow around it stays streamline.
accept: small sphere moving slowly
flow around the sphere stays streamline
stokes law needs streamline flow
conditions for stokes law
reject: F equals eta A dv dx

steps.memory_tip: Small sphere, slow motion, streamline flow — that is when Stokes' law applies.

steps.label: Stokes' law — the formula
lines: For a sphere of radius r moving
with velocity v through a fluid of
coefficient of viscosity η, the
viscous drag is
F is the viscous drag force, η the
coefficient of viscosity of the
fluid, r the radius of the sphere
and v its velocity relative to the
fluid.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Give the boxed formula and name every symbol: F, η, r, v.
steps.why: Naming every symbol is what turns the formula into something that can be applied to the raindrop in the steps that follow.
common_mistakes: Writing F = 6πrηv with a symbol left unnamed.
Forgetting the factor of 6π and writing F = πηrv.

recall.must_convey: That Stokes' law gives the viscous drag as F equals six pi eta r v, with F the drag force, eta the coefficient of viscosity, r the radius of the sphere and v its velocity.
accept: F equals six pi eta r v
drag force on a sphere
name every symbol in stokes law
six pi eta r v
reject: v t equals two ninths r squared g rho minus sigma over eta

steps.memory_tip: Six pi eta r v — every letter named: drag, viscosity, radius, velocity.

steps.label: Forces on a falling raindrop
lines: As a raindrop falls through air,
three forces act on it: its
weight, downward; the upthrust of
the air, upward; and the viscous
drag of the air, upward, given by
Stokes' law.
The drag grows as the drop's speed
grows.
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Name all three forces and their directions, and say the drag grows with speed.
steps.why: The whole derivation is a balance of these three forces, so stating them first sets up everything that follows.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the upthrust and treating the fall as only weight against drag.
Forgetting to say the drag increases as the drop speeds up — this is why a terminal speed is reached at all.

recall.must_convey: That a falling raindrop has three forces acting on it: weight downward, upthrust upward, and viscous drag upward, which grows as the speed grows.
accept: weight, upthrust and drag
three forces on the raindrop
drag increases with speed
upthrust acts upward, drag acts upward
reject: v t is proportional to r squared

steps.memory_tip: Three forces: weight down, upthrust up, drag up and growing.

steps.label: Weight and upthrust in terms of r
lines: For a raindrop of radius r and
density ρ, falling through air of
density σ, the volume of the drop
is
so its weight and the upthrust on
it are
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Write both weight and upthrust using the same volume (4/3)πr³, with ρ the drop's density and σ the air's.
steps.why: Writing both forces from the same volume is what lets them combine cleanly into the (ρ − σ) term in the balance that follows.
common_mistakes: Using the drop's density for both weight and upthrust — the upthrust uses the density of air, σ.
Forgetting the factor (4/3)π and treating the volume as r³ alone.

recall.must_convey: That the raindrop's weight is (4/3)πr³ρg and the upthrust is (4/3)πr³σg, using the same volume with the drop's density ρ and the air's density σ.
accept: weight equals four thirds pi r cubed rho g
upthrust equals four thirds pi r cubed sigma g
same volume, drop density and air density
rho is the drop, sigma is the air
reject: F equals six pi eta r v

steps.memory_tip: Same volume, two densities: ρ for the drop's weight, σ for the air's upthrust.

steps.label: Balancing the three forces
lines: As the drop speeds up, the drag
grows until it balances the net
downward force:
Once this balance is reached the
net force on the drop is zero, and
it falls at a constant speed, the
terminal velocity v_t.
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Write the balance equation and say the net force is zero once it holds.
steps.why: This is the moment the drop stops accelerating — stating the balance explicitly is what justifies calling the resulting speed constant.
common_mistakes: Balancing only weight against drag and leaving out the upthrust.
Saying the drop stops moving at this point — it keeps falling, at a constant speed, not zero speed.

recall.must_convey: That as the drop speeds up the drag grows until it balances weight minus upthrust, six pi eta r v t equals four thirds pi r cubed rho minus sigma g, and the drop then falls at a constant terminal velocity.
accept: six pi eta r v t equals four thirds pi r cubed rho minus sigma g
drag balances weight minus upthrust
net force becomes zero
the drop falls at a constant speed
reject: eta equals F over A dv dx
heard_as: six pi eta r v t

steps.memory_tip: Drag grows until it matches weight minus upthrust — then the speed stops changing.

steps.label: Terminal velocity and its r² law
lines: Solving the balance equation for
v_t,
Since v_t is proportional to r², a
large drop falls faster than a
small one.
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. Give the boxed formula for v_t and state that it goes as r², so larger drops fall faster.
steps.why: The r² dependence is the physical payoff of the whole derivation — it is what explains why raindrops of different sizes fall at different terminal speeds.
common_mistakes: Solving for v_t but never stating how it depends on r.
Losing the factor 2/9 while rearranging 6πηrv_t = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g.

recall.must_convey: That solving the balance equation gives v t equals two ninths r squared g times rho minus sigma over eta, and that v t is proportional to r squared, so a larger drop falls faster.
accept: v t equals two ninths r squared g rho minus sigma over eta
terminal velocity goes as r squared
a larger drop falls faster
boxed formula for terminal velocity
reject: F equals six pi eta r v

steps.memory_tip: v_t goes as r squared: double the radius, four times the terminal speed.

insider_note: The terminal velocity falls out of one balance equation once weight, upthrust and drag are all written from the same volume (4/3)πr³ — keep ρ (the drop) and σ (the air) from swapping places.
